newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn's dogma on EMU could turn to pragmatism in 98.
newsitem.headline: Bonn's dogma on EMU could turn to pragmatism in 98.

text.p: Germany is not about to relax its campaign of relentless insistence that the Maastricht criteria be met to the letter, but some officials are admitting privately that small transgressions may have to be tolerated.

Rumours that Germany and France would strike a deal this week to lower the standards set for entry to European monetary union were firmly denied by Bonn on Monday on the eve of a meeting of the finance ministers of the two countries.

But the official denials mask growing tacit acceptance of the idea that three percent -- the Maastricht Treaty's magic number for budget deficits as a percentage of growth -- may not have to mean that 3.0 percent is the absolute ceiling.

Germany has been by far the most vocal of the 15 European Union countries in insisting that the three percent reference value for deficits compared to Gross Domestic product must be taken to mean a maximum of 3.0 percent and not 3.1 or above.
Bonn implicitly extends this hardline approach to the goals on interest and exchange rates, inflation and public debt, with its repeated insistence that the criteria must not be weakened.
Data from 1997 will be used to establish each country's eligiblity for EMU by EU heads of government in early 1998.

Monday's German denial came from foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel who stressed that there was no question of the EMU criteria being softened, reiterating the hardline approach propagated by Finance Minister Theo Waigel.
"There will be no divergence from the stability criteria," Kinkel said in a statement. "Rumours of such considerations are totally baseless."

But this public stance, aimed at reassuring nervous German citizens that the new single currency will be as stable as their beloved mark, comes despite the fact that even the Treaty itself allows some scope for flexibility.
On the fiscal criteria in particular, the Treaty expressly allows looser guidelines to be applied if weak economic conditions trigger higher budget spending.
One Bonn source familiar with EU issues made clear that this scope opened by the Treaty for a small degree of flexibility was tacitly recognised in government circles.
"The treaty allows room for interpretation on the deficit and debt issues," he said.
"If necessary the leaders will talk about that possibility. But the Treaty itself makes clear the goal can be three percent plus x, where x is only a very small number."

The source was commenting after a series of statements from the Bundesbank last week on the way in which the budget criteria -- the most tricky of the series of economic conditions laid down in the Treaty -- should be interpreted.

At a symposium last Thursday, even Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, a staunch defender of the need for a firm economic basis for the new Euro, seemed to signal by omission that Germany could be starting to think a little more flexibly.
In remarks which deviated notably from the standard German line, he declined to insist the Maastricht reference limits on public deficits and debt must be taken as absolute maximums.

Instead, Tietmeyer confined his remarks to stressing that the quality of the country's fiscal health was the most important issue, coupled with the ability to keep deficits and borrowing under control long term.

The Bonn source confirmed that this meshed with government thinking. "The level of fiscal stability long-term will be the key," the source said. "1997 data will have a heavy weighting in the decision but they will not be the only factor."
Separately, Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke referred openly in a speech to flexibility in interpreting the criteria, although he warned that this scope was only limited.
In a third Bundesbank comment, board member Edgar Meister last week urged the European Monetary Institute and the European Commission to give a binding interpretation of the Treaty.

But official confirmation from Bonn of the limits it would tolerate are likely to remain elusive, with the flexibility offered by the Treaty seen even privately as a margin for error rather an excuse for countries to lower their sights.
"No one is going to say whether 3.1 percent is acceptable and 3.2 percent not," a second German source said. "This will all be decided in 1998."
